en.text: By the number of ovaries and flowers that form them, fruits are simple, aggregate or multiple. A simple fruit comes from one ovary of one flower (apple, grape, citrus); an aggregate fruit from many ovaries of one flower on one receptacle (strawberry); a multiple fruit from the ovaries of several flowers united into a mass (pineapple). Simple fruits are fleshy or dry, and dry fruits are dehiscent (split open) or indehiscent (do not split).

screens.title: Kinds of simple fruit
paras: The pericarp is the fruit wall.
Fleshy fruit: pericarp fleshy at maturity, e.g. grape, banana.
Dry fruit: pericarp dry at maturity, e.g. coconut, peanut.
Dry fruits split further into two kinds.
Dehiscent: splits open when mature, e.g. a mustard pod (silique).
Indehiscent: does not split open, e.g. sunflower.
screens.note: The book lists these four as equal groups and gives "pome" (apple) as an indehiscent example. Dehiscent and indehiscent are kinds of DRY fruit; apple is fleshy.

en.text: By temperature need, tropical fruits grow in a year-round summer-like season without freezing (banana, pineapple, papaya, mango, guava). Sub-tropical fruits cannot tolerate severe winters but need some winter chilling (citrus, figs, olives). Temperate fruits need a cold winter plus a summer growing season and survive temperatures well below freezing (apples, cherries, peaches).

en.text: By ripening, climacteric fruits show a rise in respiration and in ethylene production; ethylene triggers and coordinates their ripening (tomato, apple, pear, melon). Non-climacteric fruits lack this ethylene-linked respiration peak (grape, orange, pineapple). Climacteric fruits can be picked mature and ripen later, but non-climacteric fruits should be picked ripe.

ideas.name: Tree fruits, small fruits and using the four systems

en.text: By plant characteristics, tree fruits grow on trees (peach, plum, mango, citrus, avocado, guava, coffee, apple) and small fruits grow on shrubs (blackberry, raspberry, blueberry). Every fruit can be described in all four systems at once: an apple is a simple, temperate, climacteric tree fruit; an orange is a simple, sub-tropical, non-climacteric tree fruit.

notes.text: p.24–25: the book lists fleshy, dry, dehiscent and indehiscent as four equal groups. Dehiscent and indehiscent are kinds of DRY fruit; "silique" is a fruit type (mustard pod), and "pome" (apple) is fleshy, a poor indehiscent example. The lesson teaches the corrected structure.
p.26: mango is listed twice in the tree-fruit examples. p.27: there is no Activity 2.1 or Brainstorming 2.2; numbering jumps to Activity 2.2.
